stem: In Tessellate 4, an operator sets ferry.eager = true on a ferry that sends a 3 MB payload into a receiving lane. The receiving lane has 4 tiles, and the operator expects it to run for 10 beats. With eager off, that lane's billing weight would be 4 × 10 = 40. What should the operator expect?
options: {'A': "Latency drops, the receiving lane's billing weight becomes 80, and the payload arrives as shards that may be out of order and are not reordered.", 'B': "Latency drops, the receiving lane stays at 40, and the sending lane's billing weight doubles instead.", 'C': "Latency drops, the receiving lane's billing weight becomes 80, and eager mode makes Tessellate reorder the shards before delivery.", 'D': 'The ferry is rejected because eager ferries cannot carry payloads larger than 2 MB.'}
rationale: Eager ferries double the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane, and payloads over 2 MB are split into shards that Tessellate does not reorder.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a downstream tile receives records from another lane through a ferry. When the ferry carries about 1 MB, the records always arrive in the correct order. When it carries about 5 MB, the records sometimes arrive scrambled. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': "The ferry beat is too short, so the second beat overwrites part of the first beat's data.", 'B': 'The receiving lane holds more than 7 tiles, so some tiles read the data late.', 'C': 'Ferries larger than 2 MB are split into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not put them back in order.', 'D': 'The trace flag is recording outputs, and this changes the order of the ferry contents.'}
rationale: Ferries over 2 MB are sharded, shards may arrive out of order, and Tessellate never reorders them, so only the large transfers come out scrambled.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile runs in an unpinned lane with retry.limit set to 6. After its first failure, an upstream tile corrects the data the failed tile depends on. Every retry still fails. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The tile retries 3 times with back-off, using the corrected upstream data, and then the whole run fails.', 'B': 'The tile retries 6 times immediately with no back-off, each time using its original inputs, and then only that lane fails.', 'C': 'The tile retries 6 times with normal back-off, using the corrected upstream data, and then only that lane fails.', 'D': 'The tile retries 6 times immediately with no back-off, using its original inputs, and then the whole run fails.'}
rationale: A retry limit above 5 disables back-off, retries always reuse the original inputs, and a failure in an unpinned lane fails only that lane.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile failed because an upstream tile supplied bad data. The upstream data has now been fixed, but the tile's automatic retries keep failing in the same way. What should the operator do so the work runs on the corrected data?
options: {'A': 'Raise retry.limit above 5 so the retries fire immediately and pick up the corrected data.', 'B': 'Restore a snapshot of the lane so the retries re-read their inputs from scratch.', 'C': 'Run ledger.compact so the retry history is cleared and the next retry reloads its inputs.', 'D': 'Stop relying on retries and launch a fresh run of the tile after the upstream fix, because retries always reuse the original inputs.'}
rationale: Retries always reuse the tile's original inputs even after upstream data changes, so only a fresh run of the tile will read the corrected data.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a lane named _audit has 3 tiles. It must run on every beat for 30 consecutive beats. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Pin _audit once at the start, with its 3 tiles, and leave the pin in place for the full 30 beats.', 'B': 'Leave _audit unpinned with 3 tiles, because a lane with fewer than 7 tiles is always scheduled.', 'C': 'Pin _audit with its 3 tiles, and renew the pin with pin.renew before each 12-beat expiry throughout the 30 beats.', 'D': 'Pin _audit and add 2 more tiles to it, so the lane has 5 tiles to absorb the extra work.'}
rationale: Underscore lanes run only when pinned, pinned lanes are capped at 3 tiles, and pins expire after 12 beats unless they are renewed, so the pin must be renewed to cover 30 beats.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a pinned lane named _reports ran on every beat, and its pin was renewed regularly with pin.renew. Yesterday the operator upgraded Tessellate to a new version. Since the upgrade, _reports has not run at all, and no error was reported. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The upgrade reset all pins, and because _reports starts with an underscore, the scheduler cannot see it unless it is pinned.', 'B': 'The lane passed 7 tiles, so the scheduler quietly rejected the whole lane.', 'C': 'The pin hit its 12-beat expiry, because pin.renew does not work on underscore lanes.', 'D': 'A gate in the lane is checked continuously and is holding every tile in a blocked state.'}
rationale: Upgrading Tessellate resets all pins, and an underscore lane never runs unless it is pinned, so the lane silently stopped.

stem: In Tessellate 4, lane A and lane B each hold 3 tiles and are each half full. Both lanes run for 20 beats. They exchange data through a ferry that has ferry.eager = true. Which change will reduce total billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Run ledger.compact after every beat so less history is kept.', 'B': 'Split the two lanes into four lanes so that each tile has more room.', 'C': 'Keep the two lanes, and set retry.limit above 5 so failed tiles finish faster.', 'D': 'Merge lanes A and B into one lane of 6 tiles, which also removes the need for the eager ferry.'}
rationale: Merging two half-full lanes reduces billing weight, and removing the eager ferry also removes its doubling of the receiving lane's weight, while compacting and splitting never reduce weight.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a team lists its assumptions about costs. Which assumption is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Idle tiles in a lane that is running still add to billing weight.', 'B': 'Running ledger.compact every week will lower our billing weight.', 'C': 'Turning on ferry.eager doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane.', 'D': 'Splitting one lane into two lanes will never reduce billing weight.'}
rationale: ledger.compact reduces stored history but does not reduce billing weight.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an unpinned lane already holds 7 tiles. An operator submits an 8th tile to the same lane. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The submission is rejected with a capacity error.', 'B': 'Tessellate automatically creates a second lane and places the 8th tile there.', 'C': 'The 8th tile is placed in a queue without any warning or error.', 'D': 'The oldest tile in the lane is removed to make room for the new tile.'}
rationale: A lane holds at most 7 tiles, and an 8th tile is silently queued rather than rejected.

stem: In Tessellate 4, six tiles must repeatedly share an 8 MB dataset. The records must stay in order, and the cost should stay low. The tiles do not need to run on every beat. Which layout fits best?
options: {'A': 'Put all six tiles in one ordinary unpinned lane, so they share the data through lane memory.', 'B': 'Put each tile in its own lane, and connect the lanes with eager ferries to keep latency low.', 'C': 'Put all six tiles in one pinned lane, so the shared data is always available.', 'D': 'Put all six tiles in a lane named _shared, so other lanes cannot reach the data.'}
rationale: Tiles in the same lane share memory, and six tiles fit under the 7-tile limit, which avoids out-of-order ferry shards, eager-ferry billing doubling, the 3-tile pinned cap and the never-run underscore lane.

stem: An agent has two tools. search_customers(name) returns matching customer records with their numeric IDs. get_customer(customer_id) expects a numeric ID. In the logs, the agent often calls get_customer with a customer's name, such as "Dana Lee", and gets back only "Error 400". It then repeats the same call several times until it hits the step limit. What is the most effective fix?
options: {'A': "Raise the agent's step limit so it has more attempts to recover from the failed call.", 'B': 'Lower the sampling temperature so the agent produces more deterministic tool calls.', 'C': 'Make get_customer return an error that says it needs a numeric ID and that search_customers can find the ID from a name.', 'D': 'Add a system prompt rule that tells the agent never to call the same tool twice in a row.'}
rationale: An actionable error message tells the model exactly what went wrong and which tool to use next, which breaks the retry loop at its cause.

stem: An assistant has two tools. get_weather is described as "Gets weather data for a location." get_forecast is described as "Retrieves weather information." Users who ask about tomorrow often get today's conditions, because the model keeps choosing get_weather. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The two descriptions overlap and neither one says when to use it, such as current conditions versus future days.', 'B': 'The model has too few tools available to tell the difference between weather-related requests.', 'C': 'The tool names use snake_case, which models parse less reliably than camelCase.', 'D': 'The sampling temperature is too low, so the model always picks the first matching tool.'}
rationale: The model chooses tools based on their descriptions, so two vague and overlapping descriptions leave it no basis for picking the forecast tool for future dates.

stem: A developer's system prompt begins with the line "Current time: {timestamp to the second}". After that line come about 20,000 tokens of fixed product documentation, and a cache breakpoint is set at the end of the documentation. The user message after the breakpoint is different on every request. Requests arrive every 30 seconds, yet the usage data shows zero cached input tokens on every call. What explains this?
options: {'A': 'The cache lifetime expires between requests, so each entry is evicted before it can be reused.', 'B': 'The cached section is shorter than the minimum length required for caching.', 'C': 'The user message changes on every request, which invalidates the cached documentation.', 'D': 'The timestamp changes on every request and sits before the breakpoint, so the cached prefix is never identical.'}
rationale: Cache matching requires an exact match of the prefix up to the breakpoint, so a timestamp that changes every request at the start of the prompt prevents any hit, while content after the breakpoint does not matter.

stem: Each request to an app contains four parts: fixed instructions that are the same for everyone, a 30,000-token policy manual shared by all users, a short profile for the current user, and the user's conversation so far. Which layout minimizes input cost through prompt caching?
options: {'A': 'Put the user profile first, then the instructions, then the manual, then the conversation, with a breakpoint after the manual.', 'B': 'Put the instructions first, then the manual, with a breakpoint after the manual, followed by the user profile and then the conversation.', 'C': 'Put the conversation first so the newest content is cached, then the instructions, manual and profile.', 'D': 'Put the instructions, manual, profile and conversation in that order, with a single breakpoint at the very end of the conversation only.'}
rationale: Placing the content shared by all users at the front and ending the cached prefix before per-user data lets every user's requests reuse the same large cached prefix.

stem: An email assistant reads a user's inbox to write summaries. It also has a send_email tool and can read the user's contacts. An attacker sends an email containing hidden instructions to forward the inbox to an outside address. Which mitigation gives the strongest protection?
options: {'A': 'Add a system prompt line telling the model to ignore any instructions found inside emails.', 'B': 'Remove send capability from the step that reads untrusted email content, and require explicit user confirmation for any outgoing email.', 'C': 'Wrap each email in clearly labelled delimiters so the model can tell data apart from instructions.', 'D': 'Run a classifier that blocks emails containing phrases such as "ignore previous instructions".'}
rationale: Limiting what the model can do while it processes untrusted text, and gating harmful actions behind a human, still holds even when the injection succeeds, whereas prompt wording, delimiters and phrase filters can all be bypassed.

stem: A research assistant runs four steps. Which step creates the prompt-injection risk that an attacker who controls a web page can exploit?
options: {'A': "Step 1: The user's question is checked against a maximum length before processing.", 'B': 'Step 2: Web search results are limited to pages served over HTTPS.', 'C': "Step 3: Fetched page text goes into the same prompt as the user's private session data and a tool that can send HTTP requests to any URL.", 'D': 'Step 4: The final answer is HTML-escaped before it is shown in the browser.'}
rationale: Putting attacker-controlled text in front of a model that holds private data and can reach arbitrary URLs lets injected instructions exfiltrate that data.

stem: A team wants to know whether prompt version 2 of their support bot gives better answers than version 1. Which evaluation method is valid?
options: {'A': 'Score both versions on the 100 examples the team used while writing version 2, since those examples are already well understood.', 'B': 'Ask an LLM judge to rate each answer, telling it which prompt version produced each answer so it has full context.', 'C': 'Treat the version with longer average answers as better, since longer answers usually contain more helpful detail.', 'D': 'Use a held-out set of representative real queries and blind pairwise judging in random order, with the judge checked against human ratings.'}
rationale: Held-out representative data, blinding, randomized order and a judge validated against humans together remove contamination, labelling bias, position bias and an unverified judge.

stem: An engineer reports that a new prompt raised accuracy from 81% to 94% on a 200-question test set. You learn that these 200 questions are the same ones the engineer used to repeatedly test and adjust the new prompt during development. What is the main flaw in this result?
options: {'A': 'The prompt was tuned on the test questions, so the score overstates how well it will do on new questions.', 'B': 'Accuracy cannot be used as a metric for language model outputs.', 'C': 'A 200-question test set is always too small to produce any meaningful result.', 'D': 'The baseline score of 81% is too high to be improved upon in a reliable way.'}
rationale: Iterating on the very questions used for scoring overfits the prompt to them, so the improvement may not generalize to unseen inputs.

stem: A legal tool must answer questions about a 2,000-page set of contracts, which is far larger than the model's context window. Answers must quote exact clauses, and many clauses refer to other numbered sections. Which strategy fits best?
options: {'A': 'Truncate the contracts to the first part that fits in the context window and answer from that text.', 'B': 'Summarize the contracts in rounds until the summary fits, then answer every question from the summary.', 'C': 'Split the contracts along section boundaries, retrieve the sections relevant to each question along with the sections they reference, and quote from the retrieved text.', 'D': 'Raise the maximum output token limit so the model can process the full contract set in a single call.'}
rationale: Structure-aware retrieval that follows cross-references keeps the exact clause wording within the window, while truncation drops content, summarization loses verbatim text, and output limits do not expand input capacity.

stem: An app places the user's question at the very top of the prompt, followed by about 150,000 tokens of documents. Answers are accurate when the relevant fact appears near the start or end of the documents but often miss facts located in the middle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {'A': 'The max_tokens setting is too low, so the answers are cut off before the facts appear.', 'B': 'The model attends less reliably to the middle of very long contexts, and putting the question before the documents makes this worse.', 'C': 'The sampling temperature is too high, which causes random errors that are unrelated to position.', 'D': 'The tokenizer drops tokens from the middle of any input longer than 100,000 tokens.'}
rationale: Recall of content in the middle of long contexts is weaker, and placing the question after the documents, or extracting relevant passages first, reduces this position-dependent loss.

stem: A 3 MB ferry sends data from lane Alpha to lane Beta with ferry.eager set to true. Beta contains four tiles and runs for five beats. Which outcome should the operator expect?
options: {'A': 'The payload remains whole, and only the tile that reads it has doubled billing weight.', 'B': 'The payload is sharded and may arrive out of order without reordering, while Beta contributes 40 units of billing weight.', 'C': 'The payload is sharded and automatically reordered, while Beta contributes 20 units of billing weight.', 'D': 'The ferry copies continuously between beats, and the tiles in Alpha receive doubled billing weight.'}
rationale: A ferry over 2 MB is sharded without automatic reordering, and eager mode doubles Beta's normal weight of four tiles times five beats from 20 to 40.

stem: A 2.6 MB record is sent through a ferry, and the receiving lane sometimes sees later sections before earlier sections. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The ferry split the record into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate did not reorder them.', 'B': 'The receiving lane exceeded seven tiles, causing Tessellate to reverse the record.', 'C': "A retry used the record's original input and rearranged its sections.", 'D': 'The metrics sampler omitted sections that arrived between sampled beats.'}
rationale: Ferries larger than 2 MB are split into shards that may arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them.

stem: A tile in a pinned lane has retry.limit set to 6 and first runs with input version 1. Immediately after its first failure, upstream data changes to version 2. What happens if the tile keeps failing?
options: {'A': 'Its retries use version 2 with normal back-off, and only the lane fails after the last retry.', 'B': 'Its retries alternate between versions 1 and 2, and the pin is removed after the last retry.', 'C': 'Its retries use version 1 without back-off, and the whole run fails if the tile remains failed.', 'D': 'Its retries use version 2 without back-off, and the tile is silently queued after the last retry.'}
rationale: Retries retain the original version 1 inputs, a limit above 5 disables back-off, and an ultimately failed tile in a pinned lane fails the whole run.

stem: A tile failed using an old upstream value, but the upstream value has now been corrected. The next execution must use the corrected value rather than the failed tile's saved input. What should the operator do?
options: {'A': 'Increase retry.limit so the next retry reloads upstream data.', 'B': 'Set ferry.eager to true before allowing the retry.', 'C': 'Compact the ledger and then resume the same retry sequence.', 'D': "Stop using that tile's retry sequence and launch a fresh tile execution after the correction."}
rationale: Every retry reuses the tile's original inputs, so a fresh tile execution is needed to obtain corrected upstream data.

stem: Four independent audit tiles must run on every beat for 30 beats, and their lane names must begin with an underscore. Which setup satisfies the requirement?
options: {'A': 'Place all four tiles in one pinned underscore lane and renew its pin after 12 beats.', 'B': 'Place all four tiles in one unpinned underscore lane and set retry.limit to 6.', 'C': 'Place the tiles in one ordinary unpinned lane so the scheduler can see them.', 'D': 'Split the tiles across two pinned underscore lanes with at most three tiles each, and renew both pins before they expire.'}
rationale: Underscore lanes must be pinned to run, pinned lanes hold at most three tiles, and their pins must be renewed because they expire after 12 beats.

stem: An underscore lane was pinned and ran normally, but it stopped after 12 beats even though no upgrade or configuration change occurred. What is the most likely explanation?
options: {'A': "The lane's pin expired because it was not renewed with pin.renew.", 'B': 'The scheduler rejected the lane because underscore lanes may run for only 12 beats.', 'C': 'The lane was automatically split because it contained more than 2 MB of data.', 'D': 'The ledger stopped the lane when its billing history reached 12 beats.'}
rationale: Pins expire after 12 beats unless they are renewed with pin.renew, and an underscore lane cannot run without a pin.

stem: A receiving lane has five tiles, including two idle tiles, and runs for six beats with ferry.eager set to true. Its billing weight is therefore 60. Which proposed change has the stated effect on billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Run ledger.compact, reducing the billing weight from 60 to 30.', 'B': 'Remove the two idle tiles while keeping the same beats and eager setting, reducing the billing weight from 60 to 36.', 'C': 'Split the lane into two lanes, guaranteeing that the billing weight falls below 60.', 'D': 'Delete the stored ledger history without changing the lane, reducing the billing weight to zero.'}
rationale: Removing the two idle tiles leaves three billed tiles, so eager billing becomes three tiles times six beats times two, or 36.

stem: Which operator statement about Tessellate billing is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Idle tiles still count toward billing weight when their lane is running.', 'B': 'Running ledger.compact lowers billing weight by deleting old history.', 'C': 'An eager ferry doubles the billing weight of every tile in its receiving lane.', 'D': 'Merging two half-full lanes into one lane reduces billing weight.'}
rationale: ledger.compact reduces stored history but does not reduce billing weight.

stem: A normal unpinned lane already contains seven tiles, and an operator adds an eighth tile. What happens to the eighth tile?
options: {'A': 'It is silently queued rather than rejected.', 'B': 'It immediately runs in a newly created lane.', 'C': 'It replaces the oldest tile in the lane.', 'D': 'It is rejected with a lane-capacity error.'}
rationale: A lane holds at most seven tiles, and an eighth tile is silently queued.

stem: Six tiles must exchange data directly through shared memory with no ferry delay, and they must remain visible to the scheduler without pin renewal. Which layout meets these requirements?
options: {'A': 'Put three tiles in each of two ordinary lanes and rely on their memories being shared.', 'B': 'Put all six tiles in one pinned ordinary lane.', 'C': 'Put all six tiles in one ordinary, non-underscore, unpinned lane.', 'D': 'Put all six tiles in one unpinned underscore lane.'}
rationale: Six tiles fit within one normal lane's seven-tile capacity, share that lane's memory, and remain scheduler-visible without pinning.

stem: An expense agent has a create_payment tool that immediately sends money. When a user says, “Pay the invoice like last month,” the agent sometimes selects the wrong invoice when several invoices match. Which tool-design change best prevents incorrect payments while preserving useful automation?
options: {'A': 'The application should increase the model temperature so the agent considers more possible invoices.', 'B': 'The application should add a longer system prompt telling the agent to be careful with ambiguous requests.', 'C': 'The application should split payment into a preparation step that returns exact payment details and an execution step requiring an idempotent confirmation token approved for those details.', 'D': 'The application should add an optional free-text field in which the agent explains why it selected the invoice.'}
rationale: Separating preparation from execution and binding confirmation to validated payment details prevents ambiguity or retries from directly causing an irreversible payment.

stem: An agent has two tools: lookup_customer, which requires an exact customer ID, and search_customers, which accepts names or email fragments. Both tool descriptions merely say, “Find a customer,” and the agent often passes names to lookup_customer. What is the most likely reason for the misuse?
options: {'A': 'The tool descriptions do not distinguish when each tool applies or what form of input each one accepts.', 'B': 'The agent needs a higher temperature to choose between tools more accurately.', 'C': 'The lookup_customer tool returns too little customer information after a successful call.', 'D': 'The tools are misused because an agent cannot reliably use more than one customer-related tool.'}
rationale: Overlapping descriptions and unclear input constraints give the model insufficient information to select the appropriate tool.

stem: A provider reuses cached prompt prefixes only when an eligible prefix is token-for-token identical to one seen previously. An application sends requests above the cache-size threshold, but almost none receive cache hits. Each request begins with a user ID and current timestamp, followed by an unchanged system policy, unchanged tool definitions, and then the user’s question. What best explains the missing hits?
options: {'A': 'The unchanged policy is too stable for the cache to store it more than once.', 'B': 'The changing user ID and timestamp alter the beginning of the prompt, so the later stable content does not form a reusable identical prefix.', 'C': 'Tool definitions are never eligible for prompt caching, even when they are unchanged.', 'D': 'Prompt caching works only when the user’s final question is identical across requests.'}
rationale: Prefix caching cannot reuse the stable policy and tools when request-specific content appears earlier and changes the prefix.

stem: An application makes many requests using the same system instructions, tool definitions, and few-shot examples, while account data and user questions vary on every request. Which prompt layout is most likely to maximize cache reuse and reduce input cost?
options: {'A': 'The application should place account data first, followed by the stable instructions and examples.', 'B': 'The application should randomly reorder the few-shot examples on each request.', 'C': 'The application should repeat the stable instructions both before and after the user’s question.', 'D': 'The application should place stable instructions, tools, and examples first, followed by request-specific account data and the user’s question.'}
rationale: A long stable prefix followed by changing content maximizes the portion that prefix-based caching can reuse.

stem: A research agent reads arbitrary web pages and has tools for accessing internal records and sending HTTP requests. A malicious page instructs the agent to copy internal records to an external URL. Which mitigation provides the strongest protection against this prompt-injection attack?
options: {'A': 'The system prompt should state in capital letters that web pages must never override the agent’s instructions.', 'B': 'The application should enforce least-privilege tool access with deterministic authorization rules, restrict outbound destinations, and require approval for sensitive data transfers.', 'C': 'The application should ask the same model whether each proposed tool call appears suspicious before executing it.', 'D': 'The application should remove sentences containing phrases such as “ignore previous instructions” from fetched pages.'}
rationale: Enforced capability and authorization boundaries limit harmful actions even when untrusted content successfully influences the model.

stem: A support pipeline fetches customer ticket text, asks one model to summarize it, inserts that summary as a developer message for a planning model, and lets the planner call account-management tools. An attacker places instructions in a ticket that survive summarization and influence the planner. Which pipeline step creates the exploitable trust-boundary failure?
options: {'A': 'The pipeline fetches the ticket before it knows which account-management tool will be needed.', 'B': 'The summarizer produces fewer tokens than the original customer ticket.', 'C': 'The pipeline promotes a summary derived from untrusted ticket text into a privileged developer-message channel.', 'D': 'The planning model receives descriptions of the available account-management tools.'}
rationale: Treating model-processed untrusted content as privileged instructions allows injected content to gain authority in the planning step.

stem: A team wants to determine whether a new tool-using agent completes production support tasks more reliably than the current agent despite nondeterministic model outputs. Which evaluation method is most valid?
options: {'A': 'The team should run both agents once on ten handpicked examples and compare which responses look more polished.', 'B': 'The team should ask the new agent to grade its own outputs and report its average confidence.', 'C': 'The team should deploy the new agent to all users and compare raw completion counts with the previous month.', 'D': 'The team should use a representative held-out task set in a controlled tool sandbox, run paired repeated trials, score task success with predefined checks, and report uncertainty.'}
rationale: Representative held-out tasks, controlled conditions, repeated paired trials, objective criteria, and uncertainty estimates support a valid comparison.

stem: A team tries 30 prompt variants on the same 200-ticket benchmark, selects the variant with the highest score, and then reports its three-point gain on that benchmark as final test performance. What is the main flaw in the result?
options: {'A': 'The benchmark became part of the tuning process, so the reported best score is likely optimistically biased by test-set leakage and repeated selection.', 'B': 'A prompt evaluation is invalid unless every model response is generated with a temperature of zero.', 'C': 'A three-point gain is automatically meaningless whenever fewer than one thousand tickets are evaluated.', 'D': 'The team should have selected the prompt variant with the longest average response instead.'}
rationale: Repeatedly selecting variants on the benchmark overfits the evaluation set, so an untouched test set is needed for an unbiased final estimate.

stem: A contract-analysis application must answer questions about rare clauses and their cross-references across documents that are too large to fit in one context window. Which strategy best preserves relevant detail while controlling context size?
options: {'A': 'The application should keep only the first and last pages of every contract because important terms usually appear there.', 'B': 'The application should create one short summary of each entire contract and discard the source text before answering questions.', 'C': 'The application should use section-aware indexing, decompose the question, retrieve and rerank relevant sections with neighboring and referenced sections, and retain citations to the source text.', 'D': 'The application should reserve more output tokens, even if that requires truncating additional input documents.'}
rationale: Structured retrieval with query decomposition and cross-reference expansion selects detailed evidence without requiring all source documents to fit in one prompt.

stem: An assistant’s answers become less accurate as conversations grow, even though the total prompt remains just under the model’s context limit. Logs show that the prompt contains the full chat history, several duplicated retrieval results, and key instructions buried near the middle. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The model stops processing input as soon as the prompt exceeds half of its advertised context window.', 'B': 'Excess and duplicated context is competing with relevant evidence, while important information in the middle is harder for the model to use reliably.', 'C': 'The assistant is inaccurate because context windows can contain only user messages and not retrieved documents.', 'D': 'The assistant needs a larger maximum output-token setting to understand the earlier input.'}
rationale: Being within the nominal limit does not prevent irrelevant context, duplication, and middle-position effects from degrading attention to important information.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an operator sets ferry.eager = true on a ferry that sends a 3 MB payload into a receiving lane. The receiving lane has 4 tiles and is expected to run for 10 beats. With eager off, that lane's billing weight would be 4 × 10 = 40. What should the operator expect?
options: {'A': 'Latency rises, and the receiving lane stays at 40, because eager mode only changes the billing weight of the sending lane.', 'B': "Latency drops, the receiving lane's billing weight doubles to 80, and the 3 MB payload is split into shards that may arrive out of order and are not reordered.", 'C': "Latency drops, the receiving lane's billing weight halves to 20, and eager mode reorders the shards before delivery.", 'D': 'The ferry is rejected, because eager ferries cannot carry payloads larger than 2 MB.'}
rationale: Eager ferries lower latency but double the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane, and payloads over 2 MB are split into shards that Tessellate does not reorder.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a downstream tile receives records from another lane through a ferry. When the ferry carries about 1 MB, the records always arrive in order. When it carries about 5 MB, the records sometimes arrive scrambled. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The ferry beat is too long, so Tessellate merges two beats of data into one transfer.', 'B': 'The receiving lane holds more than 7 tiles, so the extra tiles are rejected and the data shifts.', 'C': 'The trace flag is recording the ferry outputs, and this changes the order of the records.', 'D': 'Ferries larger than 2 MB are split into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not put the shards back in order.'}
rationale: Only ferries over 2 MB are sharded, and Tessellate never reorders shards, so only the large transfers arrive scrambled.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile runs in an unpinned lane with retry.limit set to 6. After the tile's first failure, an upstream tile corrects the data the failed tile depends on. Every retry still fails. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The tile retries 6 times immediately with no back-off, each time reusing its original inputs, and then only that lane fails.', 'B': 'The tile retries 3 times with back-off, using the corrected upstream data, and then the whole run fails.', 'C': 'The tile retries 6 times with normal back-off, using the corrected upstream data, and then the whole run fails.', 'D': 'The tile does not retry at all, because a retry limit above 5 turns retries off.'}
rationale: A retry limit above 5 disables back-off so retries fire immediately, retries always reuse the original inputs, and a failure in an unpinned lane fails only that lane.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile failed because an upstream tile supplied bad data. The upstream data has now been fixed, but the tile's automatic retries keep failing in the same way. What should the operator do so the work runs on the corrected data?
options: {'A': 'Raise retry.limit above 5, so the retries fire faster and pick up the corrected data.', 'B': 'Run ledger.compact, so the retry history is cleared and the next retry reloads its inputs.', 'C': "Launch a fresh run of the tile after the upstream fix, because retries always reuse the tile's original inputs.", 'D': 'Turn on the trace flag, so the retries record and refresh their inputs on the next beat.'}
rationale: Retries always reuse the tile's original inputs even after upstream data changes, so only a fresh run will read the corrected data.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a lane named _audit has 3 tiles. It must run on every beat for 30 consecutive beats. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Leave _audit unpinned with its 3 tiles, because any lane with fewer than 7 tiles is always scheduled.', 'B': 'Pin _audit with its 3 tiles, and renew the pin with pin.renew before each 12-beat expiry for the full 30 beats.', 'C': 'Pin _audit once at the start, because a pin lasts until the run ends.', 'D': 'Pin _audit and raise it to 7 tiles, because pinned lanes keep the normal 7-tile limit.'}
rationale: Underscore lanes run only when pinned, pinned lanes are capped at 3 tiles, and pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed with pin.renew.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a pinned lane named _reports ran on every beat, and its pin was renewed regularly with pin.renew. Yesterday the operator upgraded Tessellate to a new version. Since the upgrade, _reports has not run at all, and no error was reported. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The lane passed 7 tiles, so the scheduler rejected the whole lane with a hidden error.', 'B': 'A gate in the lane is checked continuously and is holding every tile in a blocked state.', 'C': 'The new version made the pin permanent, and permanent pins pause underscore lanes.', 'D': 'The upgrade reset all pins, and an underscore lane like _reports never runs unless it is pinned.'}
rationale: Upgrading Tessellate resets all pins, and underscore lanes are invisible to the scheduler unless pinned, so the lane silently stopped.

stem: In Tessellate 4, lane A and lane B each hold 3 tiles and are each half full. Both lanes run for 20 beats and exchange data through a ferry with ferry.eager = true. Which change will reduce total billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Merge lanes A and B into one lane of 6 tiles, which reduces billing weight and removes the need for the eager ferry.', 'B': 'Run ledger.compact after every beat, so less stored history counts toward billing weight.', 'C': 'Split the two lanes into four lanes, so each lane carries fewer tiles.', 'D': 'Keep both lanes and set retry.limit above 5, so failed tiles finish sooner.'}
rationale: Merging two half-full lanes reduces billing weight, and removing the eager ferry removes its doubling, while compacting and splitting never reduce weight.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a team lists its assumptions about costs. Which assumption is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Idle tiles in a lane that is running still add to billing weight.', 'B': 'Turning on ferry.eager doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane.', 'C': 'Running ledger.compact every week will lower our billing weight.', 'D': 'Splitting one lane into two lanes will never reduce billing weight.'}
rationale: ledger.compact reduces stored history but does not reduce billing weight.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an unpinned lane already holds 7 tiles. An operator submits an 8th tile to the same lane. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The submission is rejected with a capacity error.', 'B': 'The 8th tile is silently queued, with no warning or error.', 'C': 'Tessellate automatically creates a second lane and places the 8th tile there.', 'D': 'The oldest tile in the lane is removed to make room for the new tile.'}
rationale: A lane holds at most 7 tiles, and an 8th tile is silently queued rather than rejected.

stem: In Tessellate 4, six tiles must repeatedly share an 8 MB dataset. The records must stay in order, and cost should stay low. The tiles do not need to run on every beat. Which layout fits best?
options: {'A': 'Put each tile in its own lane, and connect the lanes with eager ferries to keep latency low.', 'B': 'Put all six tiles in one pinned lane, so the shared data is always available.', 'C': 'Put all six tiles in a lane named _shared, so other lanes cannot reach the data.', 'D': 'Put all six tiles in one ordinary unpinned lane, so they share the data through lane memory without any ferry.'}
rationale: Tiles in the same lane share memory and six tiles fit under the 7-tile limit, which avoids out-of-order ferry shards, eager billing doubling, the 3-tile pinned cap and the never-run underscore lane.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an operator sets ferry.eager = true on a ferry that sends a 3 MB payload into a receiving lane. The receiving lane has 4 tiles, and the operator expects it to run for 10 beats. With eager off, that lane's billing weight would be 4 × 10 = 40. What should the operator expect?
options: {'A': "Latency drops, the receiving lane's billing weight becomes 80, and the payload arrives as shards that may be out of order and are not reordered.", 'B': "Latency rises, and the receiving lane's billing weight falls to 20 because eager ferries are billed at a discount.", 'C': "Latency drops, the receiving lane's billing weight stays at 40, and the payload arrives as a single unsplit block.", 'D': 'The ferry is rejected because eager ferries cannot carry payloads larger than 2 MB.'}
rationale: Eager ferries double the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane, and payloads over 2 MB are split into shards that Tessellate does not reorder.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a downstream tile receives records from another lane through a ferry. When the ferry carries about 1 MB, the records always arrive in the correct order. When it carries about 5 MB, the records sometimes arrive scrambled. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'Ferries reverse the order of their records on every second beat, whatever their size.', 'B': 'The receiving lane is unpinned, and unpinned lanes shuffle incoming records at random.', 'C': 'Ferries larger than 2 MB are split into shards that can arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not put them back in order.', 'D': 'The trace flag is recording outputs, and this rewrites the order of the ferry contents.'}
rationale: Ferries over 2 MB are sharded, shards may arrive out of order, and Tessellate never reorders them, so only the large transfers come out scrambled.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile runs in an unpinned lane with retry.limit set to 6. After its first failure, an upstream tile corrects the data the failed tile depends on. Every retry still fails. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The tile retries 3 times with back-off, using the corrected upstream data, and then the whole run fails.', 'B': 'The tile retries 6 times immediately with no back-off, each time using its original inputs, and then only that lane fails.', 'C': 'The tile does not retry at all, because any retry.limit above 5 is treated as invalid and set to zero.', 'D': 'The tile retries 6 times with extra-long back-off, using the corrected upstream data, and then the whole run fails.'}
rationale: A retry limit above 5 disables back-off, retries always reuse the original inputs, and a failure in an unpinned lane fails only that lane.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile failed because an upstream tile supplied bad data. The upstream data has now been fixed, but the tile's automatic retries keep failing in the same way. What should the operator do so the work runs on the corrected data?
options: {'A': 'Simply wait, because each automatic retry reloads its inputs and will soon pick up the corrected data.', 'B': 'Run ledger.compact so the retry history is cleared and the next retry reloads its inputs.', 'C': 'Raise retry.limit above 5 so that retries switch to reading the latest upstream data.', 'D': 'Stop relying on retries and launch a fresh run of the tile after the upstream fix, because retries always reuse the original inputs.'}
rationale: Retries always reuse the tile's original inputs even after upstream data changes, so only a fresh run of the tile will read the corrected data.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a lane named _audit has 3 tiles. It must run on every beat for 30 consecutive beats. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Leave _audit unpinned, because lanes whose names start with an underscore are scheduled first on every beat.', 'B': 'Pin _audit once at the start and leave it, because a pin lasts until it is removed by hand.', 'C': 'Pin _audit with its 3 tiles, and renew the pin with pin.renew before each 12-beat expiry throughout the 30 beats.', 'D': 'Pin _audit and add 4 more tiles, because a pinned lane can hold up to 7 tiles.'}
rationale: Underscore lanes run only when pinned, pinned lanes are capped at 3 tiles, and pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed, so the pin must be renewed to cover 30 beats.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a pinned lane named _reports ran on every beat, and its pin was renewed regularly with pin.renew. Yesterday the operator upgraded Tessellate to a new version. Since the upgrade, _reports has not run at all, and no error was reported. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The upgrade reset all pins, and because _reports starts with an underscore, the scheduler cannot see it unless it is pinned.', 'B': 'The upgrade doubled the beat length to 80 seconds, so the lane now runs only half as often.', 'C': 'The upgrade permanently deleted every lane whose name starts with an underscore, along with its tiles.', 'D': 'A gate in the lane is now checked continuously, and continuous checks always block every tile.'}
rationale: Upgrading Tessellate resets all pins, and an underscore lane never runs unless it is pinned, so the lane silently stopped.

stem: In Tessellate 4, lane A and lane B each hold 3 tiles and are each half full. Both lanes run for 20 beats. They exchange data through a ferry that has ferry.eager = true. Which change will reduce total billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Run ledger.compact after every beat, since billing weight is calculated from stored history.', 'B': 'Split the two lanes into four lanes, since smaller lanes are always billed less.', 'C': 'Add ferry.eager = true to more ferries, since eager ferries finish sooner and so cost less.', 'D': 'Merge lanes A and B into one lane of 6 tiles, which also removes the need for the eager ferry.'}
rationale: Merging two half-full lanes reduces billing weight, and removing the eager ferry also removes its doubling of the receiving lane's weight, while compacting, splitting and adding eager ferries never reduce weight.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a team lists its assumptions about costs. Which assumption is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Idle tiles in a lane that is running still add to billing weight.', 'B': 'Running ledger.compact every week will lower our billing weight, because billing weight depends on how much history we store.', 'C': 'Turning on ferry.eager doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane.', 'D': 'Splitting one lane into two lanes will never reduce billing weight.'}
rationale: ledger.compact reduces stored history but does not reduce billing weight, which depends only on tiles multiplied by beats run.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an unpinned lane already holds 7 tiles. An operator submits an 8th tile to the same lane. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The submission is rejected, and the whole lane stops until a tile is removed.', 'B': 'The entire lane is deleted because it has exceeded its capacity.', 'C': 'The 8th tile is placed in a queue without any warning or error.', 'D': 'The lane limit automatically rises to 8, and the new tile starts running at once.'}
rationale: A lane holds at most 7 tiles, and an 8th tile is silently queued rather than rejected.

stem: In Tessellate 4, six tiles must repeatedly share an 8 MB dataset. The records must stay in order, and the cost should stay low. The tiles do not need to run on every beat. Which layout fits best?
options: {'A': 'Put all six tiles in one ordinary unpinned lane, so they share the data through lane memory.', 'B': 'Put each tile in its own lane, and connect the lanes with eager ferries, which keep large payloads in order and lower cost.', 'C': 'Put all six tiles in one pinned lane, since pinned lanes can hold up to 10 tiles.', 'D': 'Put all six tiles in a lane named _shared, since the scheduler runs underscore lanes first.'}
rationale: Tiles in the same lane share memory, and six tiles fit under the 7-tile limit, which avoids out-of-order ferry shards, eager-ferry billing doubling, the 3-tile pinned cap and the never-run underscore lane.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a ferry carries a 1.5 MB payload into a pinned lane that holds 3 tiles. The operator sets ferry.eager = true and runs the receiving lane for 12 beats. What should the operator expect for the receiving lane?
options: {'A': 'Its billing weight is 36, and the payload is split into shards that may arrive out of order.', 'B': 'Its billing weight is 72, and the payload arrives in one piece because it is under the shard threshold.', 'C': 'Its billing weight is 36, because eager mode only changes latency and never changes billing.', 'D': 'Its billing weight is 72, and the payload is split into shards that Tessellate reorders on arrival.'}
rationale: Eager mode doubles the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane (3 tiles x 12 beats x 2 = 72), and a 1.5 MB ferry is under the 2 MB limit, so it is not sharded.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a ferry used to carry a 1.9 MB payload, and its records always arrived in order. After a new field was added, the payload grew to 2.3 MB, and the records now sometimes arrive out of order. The team turned on ferry.eager, but the problem continued. Which explanation accounts for both the new problem and the failed fix?
options: {'A': 'The new field changed the beat length, and eager mode cannot shorten a beat that has already been changed.', 'B': 'The receiving lane went over 7 tiles, and eager mode only affects lanes that have fewer than 7 tiles.', 'C': 'The trace flag started recording outputs, and eager mode does not affect the trace flag.', 'D': 'Payloads over 2 MB are split into shards that Tessellate never reorders, and eager mode only affects latency and billing.'}
rationale: Going past 2 MB caused sharding with no reordering, and eager mode only lowers latency and doubles billing, so it cannot restore the order.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile runs in a pinned lane with retry.limit set to exactly 5. While the tile is retrying, its upstream data is updated. Every attempt fails. What happens?
options: {'A': 'The tile retries 5 times immediately with no back-off, using the updated data, and then only its lane fails.', 'B': 'The tile retries 3 times with back-off, because the default limit of 3 overrides any setting, and then only its lane fails.', 'C': 'The tile retries 5 times with back-off, using its original inputs, and then the whole run fails.', 'D': 'The tile retries 5 times with back-off, using the updated data, and then the whole run fails.'}
rationale: A limit of 5 is not above 5, so back-off stays on, retries always reuse the original inputs, and a failure in a pinned lane fails the whole run.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a tile used all three of its default retries, and each one failed on bad upstream data. The upstream data has since been corrected. Which action will make the tile process the corrected data?
options: {'A': 'Raise retry.limit to 4 so that one more retry fires and picks up the corrected data.', 'B': 'Resubmit the tile as a fresh run now that the upstream data has been corrected.', 'C': 'Turn on ferry.eager so that the retries receive the newest ferry contents.', 'D': "Turn on the trace flag so that the tile's recorded inputs are refreshed before the next retry."}
rationale: Retries always reuse the tile's original inputs, so only a fresh run of the tile will read the corrected upstream data.

stem: In Tessellate 4, six tiles that do not need to share memory must all run on every beat for 10 beats. Which setup meets this requirement?
options: {'A': 'Split the tiles into two lanes of 3 tiles each, and pin both lanes.', 'B': 'Put all 6 tiles in one lane, and pin that lane.', 'C': 'Put all 6 tiles in one unpinned lane, because a lane with fewer than 7 tiles runs on every beat.', 'D': "Put all 6 tiles in one pinned lane, and use pin.renew at beat 10 to raise the lane's tile limit."}
rationale: A pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles, so two pinned lanes of 3 tiles are needed, and 10 beats is within the 12-beat pin life, so no renewal is required.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an operator pinned a lane named _nightly at beat 0 and never ran pin.renew. No upgrade or configuration change happened. The lane ran on every beat at first, then stopped running after beat 12, and no error was shown. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'Metrics are only sampled every 5th beat, so the lane is still running but appears idle.', 'B': 'A gate in the lane is checked continuously and has locked every tile after 12 beats.', 'C': 'The lane reached 7 tiles, so the scheduler silently rejected the whole lane.', 'D': 'The pin expired after 12 beats, and an underscore lane does not run unless it is pinned.'}
rationale: Pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed, and underscore lanes are invisible to the scheduler unless pinned, so the lane stopped silently.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a lane holds 5 tiles and runs for 30 beats. Two of those tiles do no work during the whole run and are only kept so they appear ready. Which change will reduce billing weight?
options: {'A': "Run ledger.compact at the end of each day to shrink the lane's stored history.", 'B': 'Split the lane into a lane of 3 working tiles and a separate lane of 2 idle tiles.', 'C': 'Remove the two idle tiles from the lane.', 'D': 'Turn on ferry.eager for the ferry that feeds this lane so the work finishes sooner.'}
rationale: Billing weight is tiles times beats and idle tiles in a running lane still count, so removing them reduces weight, while compacting, splitting and eager ferries do not.

stem: In Tessellate 4, a team writes down four beliefs about costs. Which belief is mistaken?
options: {'A': 'Tiles that sit idle in a running lane add nothing to billing weight because they do no work.', 'B': 'Merging two half-full lanes into one lane will reduce billing weight.', 'C': 'An eager ferry doubles the billing weight of the tiles in the lane that receives the data.', 'D': 'Compacting the ledger saves storage but leaves billing weight the same.'}
rationale: Idle tiles in a running lane still count toward billing weight.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an unpinned lane holds 6 tiles. An operator submits 3 more tiles to that lane at the same time. What happens?
options: {'A': 'All 3 new tiles are rejected, because the batch would push the lane past its limit.', 'B': 'One new tile joins the lane, and the other two are queued without any warning.', 'C': 'Tessellate creates a second lane and places all 3 new tiles there.', 'D': 'All 3 new tiles join the lane, because the limit only applies to pinned lanes.'}
rationale: A lane holds at most 7 tiles, so the 7th tile joins the lane and any further tiles are silently queued rather than rejected.

stem: In Tessellate 4, five tiles must constantly share working data in memory. Four other tiles only need a 1 MB summary from them once per beat. Cost should stay low, and none of the tiles need to run on every beat. Which layout fits best?
options: {'A': 'Put all nine tiles in one unpinned lane so that every tile shares memory.', 'B': 'Put each of the nine tiles in its own lane, and connect the lanes with ferries.', 'C': 'Put the five sharing tiles in one pinned lane, and put the four other tiles in a second lane fed by an eager ferry.', 'D': 'Put the five sharing tiles in one unpinned lane, and put the four other tiles in a second unpinned lane fed by a normal ferry.'}
rationale: The five tiles share memory in one lane without hitting the 7-tile limit, and a normal ferry delivers the 1 MB summary once per beat without sharding or eager billing doubling, while nine tiles in one lane would queue two of them and a pinned lane is capped at 3 tiles.

stem: A data-analysis agent has a run_sql tool that returns every row a query produces. On large tables, a single call can return 50,000 rows. The result fills most of the context window, and the agent then forgets the user's original question or stops partway through the task. What is the most effective fix?
options: {'A': 'Switch to a model with a larger context window so the full result sets always fit.', 'B': 'Make run_sql return a limited number of rows with the total row count and a note explaining how to filter, aggregate or request the next page.', 'C': 'Add a system prompt instruction that asks the agent to write efficient queries.', 'D': 'Pass every result through a second model call that rewrites it as a short prose summary without row values or IDs.'}
rationale: Bounding the tool's output and telling the agent how to narrow or page the results keeps the context usable while still letting the agent reach any data it needs.

stem: A booking assistant has a tool called create_booking with a parameter named date, typed only as a string with the description "The booking date." The backend expects the format YYYY-MM-DD. The model often passes values such as "next Friday" or "04/05", and these bookings fail or land on the wrong day. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The tool name is too short for the model to understand what the tool does.', 'B': 'The model cannot do date arithmetic, so it should never be given date parameters.', 'C': 'The assistant has too many tools, so the model confuses their parameters.', 'D': "The parameter's schema and description do not state the required format or give an example, so the model guesses."}
rationale: The model fills parameters from the schema and description, so an unspecified format leads to natural-language or ambiguous dates instead of the format the backend needs.

stem: An API places tool definitions before the system prompt in the cached prefix. A developer sets a cache breakpoint at the end of a long, fixed system prompt. On each request, the tool list is built by iterating over an unordered set of tool objects, so the same tools appear in a different order from one request to the next. Requests arrive every few seconds, the system prompt is long enough to cache, and its text never changes. Yet cache hits are rare. What explains this?
options: {'A': 'The tool definitions come before the breakpoint, and their changing order makes the cached prefix differ between requests.', 'B': 'The cache lifetime is too short for requests that arrive every few seconds.', 'C': 'Caching only applies to the user messages, not to the system prompt.', 'D': 'Cache hits require the user message to be identical to an earlier request.'}
rationale: A cache hit needs a byte-identical prefix up to the breakpoint, and reordering the tool definitions that sit inside that prefix changes it even though the system prompt text is the same.

stem: A chat app keeps a fixed system prompt and the full conversation history in every request. Long conversations can run for 60 turns, and the history becomes the largest part of the input. Currently the only cache breakpoint is at the end of the system prompt. Which change would reduce input cost the most?
options: {'A': 'Turn off caching, because the conversation changes every turn and cannot be reused.', 'B': 'Move the newest user message to the start of the prompt so that it is cached first.', 'C': 'On each request, also place a breakpoint at the end of the latest turn so that the earlier turns are read from cache on the next request.', 'D': 'Keep the single breakpoint after the system prompt and shorten the system prompt.'}
rationale: Advancing the breakpoint to the end of the conversation each turn lets every later request reuse the whole earlier history from cache, which covers the largest and growing share of the input.

stem: A coding agent reads public GitHub issues to fix bugs. It can run shell commands, it has access to the developer's cloud credentials, and it can push directly to the main branch. An attacker files an issue with hidden text telling the agent to upload the credentials to a remote server. Which mitigation gives the strongest protection?
options: {'A': 'Add a system prompt line saying that issue text is data and must never be treated as instructions.', 'B': 'Ask the model to restate the task in its own words before it starts working on each issue.', 'C': 'Scan each issue for the words "credentials" and "upload" and skip any issue that contains them.', 'D': 'Run the agent in a sandbox with no credentials and only allowlisted network access, and require human review before any code reaches the main branch.'}
rationale: Removing the secrets, blocking arbitrary network access and putting a human before merges limits the damage even when the injection succeeds, whereas prompt wording and keyword filters can be bypassed.

stem: A support pipeline runs four steps. A customer writes the ticket text, and the model's summary can include internal notes about other accounts. Which step lets an attacker who writes a ticket steal data?
options: {'A': "The model's summary is rendered as Markdown in an internal dashboard that loads remote images automatically.", 'B': 'Tickets are encrypted at rest in the database.', 'C': 'Support staff log in to the dashboard through single sign-on.', 'D': 'Each customer can submit at most ten tickets per hour.'}
rationale: Injected instructions can make the model emit an image link whose URL encodes private data, and loading that image automatically sends the data to the attacker's server.

stem: A team wants to measure how often their document summarizer adds claims that the source document does not support. Which evaluation method is valid?
options: {'A': 'Compute the word overlap between each summary and a reference summary written by a person.', 'B': 'Check each claim in the summary against the source document using a judge whose verdicts have been validated on a human-labelled sample.', 'C': 'Ask the summarizer model to rate its own confidence that each summary is accurate.', 'D': 'Survey users on whether they find the summaries clear and pleasant to read.'}
rationale: Directly checking each claim against the source with a judge validated against humans measures unsupported claims, while overlap, self-rated confidence and reader satisfaction do not.

stem: A team reports that their new toxicity classifier reaches 97% accuracy on a test set of 1,000 user messages. You learn that 970 of those messages are not toxic. What is the main flaw in this result?
options: {'A': 'Toxicity cannot be measured by any automated method.', 'B': 'A test set of 1,000 messages is always too large to label consistently.', 'C': 'A classifier that labels every message as not toxic would also score 97%, so accuracy alone says little about catching toxic messages.', 'D': 'The team should have reported the error rate instead, because accuracy and error rate give different conclusions.'}
rationale: With a 97% majority class, accuracy matches that of a useless baseline, so precision and recall on the toxic class are needed to judge the classifier.

stem: An agent works on a software project for many hours. Its conversation and tool outputs grow far past the context window. Decisions made early, such as the chosen database schema and rejected approaches, must still guide the work much later. Which strategy fits best?
options: {'A': 'Drop the oldest messages silently whenever the context is full and continue from the most recent ones.', 'B': 'Restart the agent with an empty context every hour and give it the original task again.', 'C': 'Raise the output token limit so the agent can write longer responses that include earlier decisions.', 'D': 'Periodically compact older turns into a summary that keeps key decisions, and keep a persistent notes file the agent can re-read, while recent turns stay verbatim.'}
rationale: Compaction plus external notes preserves the important earlier decisions in a compact form while freeing space, whereas dropping or restarting loses them and output limits do not add input capacity.

stem: A chat app sends the full conversation each turn. When the input goes over the limit, the app deletes the oldest messages first. A user set output formatting rules in their first message. After about 40 turns, the assistant stops following those rules, although its answers are otherwise fine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {'A': 'The trimming step has deleted the first message, so the formatting rules are no longer in the prompt.', 'B': 'The model gradually becomes less capable as a conversation goes on, regardless of its content.', 'C': 'The sampling temperature rises automatically in long conversations.', 'D': 'The formatting rules were cached and the cache entry has expired.'}
rationale: Trimming the oldest messages removed the instructions from the input, and lasting rules should be kept in the system prompt or kept out of the trimming window.

stem: An agent has two tools. search_customers(name) returns matching customer records with their numeric IDs. get_customer(customer_id) expects a numeric ID. In the logs, the agent often calls get_customer with a customer's name, such as "Dana Lee", and gets back only "Error 400" with no further detail. It then repeats the same call several times until it hits the step limit. What is the most effective fix?
options: {'A': "Raise the agent's step limit from 10 to 50 so it has more attempts to repeat the failed call.", 'B': 'Switch to a larger model, because the failure shows the current model cannot follow tool schemas at all.', 'C': 'Replace the bare "Error 400" with a message saying get_customer needs a numeric ID and that search_customers can look up the ID from a name.', 'D': 'Remove search_customers from the agent so it has fewer tools to choose between.'}
rationale: The agent loops because the bare error gives it nothing to act on, so an error that names the problem and the correct next tool fixes the cause directly.

stem: An assistant has two tools. get_weather is described as "Gets weather data for a location." get_forecast is described as "Retrieves weather information." Users who ask about tomorrow often get today's conditions, because the model keeps choosing get_weather. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The two descriptions say nearly the same thing, and neither states whether it covers current conditions or future days.', 'B': 'The assistant has too many tools, so the model cannot keep track of which ones exist.', 'C': 'The tool names are written in snake_case, which models cannot read correctly.', 'D': "The model has no internet access, so it cannot know what tomorrow's date is."}
rationale: Models pick tools from their descriptions, and these two vague, overlapping descriptions give no signal that get_forecast handles future dates.

stem: A developer's system prompt begins with the line "Current time: {timestamp to the second}". After that line come about 20,000 tokens of fixed product documentation, and a cache breakpoint is set at the end of the documentation. The user message after the breakpoint is different on every request. Requests arrive every 30 seconds, yet the usage data shows zero cached input tokens on every call. What explains this?
options: {'A': 'The cache lifetime is shorter than 30 seconds, so every entry expires before the next request arrives.', 'B': 'The 20,000 tokens of documentation fall below the minimum length that caching requires.', 'C': 'The user message placed after the breakpoint changes each time, which invalidates everything before it.', 'D': 'The per-second timestamp at the very start of the prompt changes on every request, so the prefix before the breakpoint is never identical.'}
rationale: A cache hit needs an exact prefix match up to the breakpoint, and a timestamp that changes every second at the top of the prompt guarantees a mismatch.

stem: Each request to an app contains four parts: fixed instructions that are the same for everyone, a 30,000-token policy manual shared by all users, a short profile for the current user, and the user's conversation so far. Which layout minimizes input cost through prompt caching?
options: {'A': 'Put the per-user profile first, then the instructions, then the manual, then the conversation, with a breakpoint after the manual.', 'B': 'Put the shared instructions first and the shared manual second, with a breakpoint after the manual, followed by the user profile and then the conversation.', 'C': 'Put the conversation first so the newest messages are cached, then the instructions, manual and profile.', 'D': 'Skip caching entirely, because content that differs between users means no part of the prompt can be reused.'}
rationale: Putting all shared content at the front and ending the cached prefix before any per-user data lets every request from every user reuse the same large cached block.

stem: An email assistant reads a user's inbox to write summaries. It also has a send_email tool and can read the user's contacts. An attacker sends an email containing hidden instructions to forward the inbox to an outside address. Which mitigation gives the strongest protection?
options: {'A': 'Add a polite system prompt line asking the model not to follow instructions found inside emails.', 'B': 'Remove send capability from the step that reads untrusted email, and require explicit user confirmation before any email is sent.', 'C': 'Switch to a larger model, since larger models are immune to prompt injection.', 'D': 'Lower the sampling temperature so the model is less likely to act on unusual instructions.'}
rationale: Removing the dangerous capability during untrusted reading and gating sends behind a human still protects the user even when an injection succeeds, unlike prompt wording or model settings.

stem: A research assistant runs four steps. Which step creates the prompt-injection risk that an attacker who controls a web page can exploit?
options: {'A': "Step 1: The user's question is checked against a maximum length before processing.", 'B': 'Step 2: Web search results are limited to pages served over HTTPS.', 'C': "Step 3: Text from fetched web pages goes into the same prompt as the user's private session data and a tool that can send HTTP requests to any URL.", 'D': 'Step 4: The final answer is HTML-escaped before it is shown in the browser.'}
rationale: Step 3 combines attacker-controlled text, private data and an unrestricted outbound tool, which lets injected instructions send that data to the attacker.

stem: A team wants to know whether prompt version 2 of their support bot gives better answers than version 1. Which evaluation method is valid?
options: {'A': 'Score both versions on the same 100 examples the team used while writing and tuning version 2.', 'B': 'Ask an LLM judge to rate each answer, and tell it which answers came from the new version so it knows what to look for.', 'C': 'Have the engineers who wrote version 2 read the outputs and vote on which version they prefer.', 'D': 'Use a held-out set of representative real queries, judged blind in random order by a judge whose ratings have been checked against human ratings.'}
rationale: Only this method avoids tuning-set contamination, labelling bias, author bias and position bias while confirming the judge agrees with humans.

stem: An engineer reports that a new prompt raised accuracy from 81% to 94% on a 200-question test set. You learn that these 200 questions are the same ones the engineer used to repeatedly test and adjust the new prompt during development. What is the main flaw in this result?
options: {'A': 'The prompt was tuned on the very questions used to score it, so the 94% likely overstates performance on new questions.', 'B': 'Accuracy can never be used as a metric for any language model output.', 'C': 'Any test set under 1,000 questions always produces meaningless results.', 'D': 'No prompt can ever reliably improve on a baseline above 80%.'}
rationale: Adjusting a prompt against its own test questions overfits it to them, so the gain may not carry over to unseen inputs.

stem: A legal tool must answer questions about a 2,000-page set of contracts, which is far larger than the model's context window. Answers must quote exact clauses, and many clauses refer to other numbered sections. Which strategy fits best?
options: {'A': 'Keep only the first pages that fit in the context window and ignore the rest of the contracts.', 'B': 'Summarize the contracts repeatedly until they fit, then answer every question, including requests for exact quotes, from the summary.', 'C': 'Split the contracts at section boundaries, retrieve the sections relevant to each question plus the sections they cross-reference, and quote from that retrieved text.', 'D': 'Raise the maximum output token limit so the model can read all 2,000 pages in one call.'}
rationale: Section-aware retrieval that follows cross-references keeps exact clause wording within the window, while the other options drop content, lose verbatim text or confuse output limits with input capacity.

stem: An app places the user's question at the very top of the prompt, followed by about 150,000 tokens of documents. Answers are accurate when the relevant fact appears near the start or end of the documents but often miss facts located in the middle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {'A': 'The max_tokens setting is too low, so every answer is cut off before it is finished.', 'B': 'The model recalls the middle of very long contexts less reliably, and placing the question before the documents makes this worse.', 'C': 'The sampling temperature is too high, causing errors that occur at random positions.', 'D': 'The tokenizer silently deletes the middle portion of any input longer than 100,000 tokens.'}
rationale: The errors follow position rather than chance, matching the known weaker recall for mid-context content, which is reduced by putting the question after the documents or extracting relevant passages first.

stem: An agent has two tools. search_customers(name) returns matching customer records with their numeric IDs. get_customer(customer_id) expects a numeric ID. In the logs, the agent often calls get_customer with a customer's name, such as "Dana Lee", and gets back only "Error 400", which gives no hint about what input was expected. The agent then repeats the same call until it hits the step limit. What is the most effective fix?
options: {'A': "Raise the agent's step limit so it has more attempts to repeat the failed call.", 'B': 'Remove search_customers so the agent has fewer tools to choose between.', 'C': 'Make get_customer return an error that says it needs a numeric ID and that search_customers can find the ID from a name.', 'D': 'Switch the error code from 400 to 500 so the agent treats it as a server problem.'}
rationale: An actionable error message tells the model what went wrong and which tool to use next, which breaks the retry loop at its cause.

stem: An assistant has two tools. get_weather is described as "Gets weather data for a location." get_forecast is described as "Retrieves weather information." Neither description mentions dates or time ranges. Users who ask about tomorrow often get today's conditions, because the model keeps choosing get_weather. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The two descriptions overlap and neither one says when to use it, such as current conditions versus future days.', 'B': 'The model needs at least five tools before it can compare tool descriptions properly.', 'C': 'The tool names use snake_case, which models cannot read as reliably as camelCase.', 'D': 'The weather service behind get_forecast is returning out-of-date data.'}
rationale: The model chooses tools based on their descriptions, so two vague and overlapping descriptions give it no basis for picking the forecast tool for future dates.

stem: A developer's system prompt begins with the line "Current time: {timestamp to the second}". After that line come about 20,000 tokens of fixed product documentation, and a cache breakpoint is set at the end of the documentation. The user message after the breakpoint is different on every request. Requests arrive every 30 seconds, well within the five-minute cache lifetime, yet the usage data shows zero cached input tokens on every call. What explains this?
options: {'A': 'The five-minute cache lifetime expires between requests that are 30 seconds apart.', 'B': 'The 20,000-token cached section is shorter than the minimum length required for caching.', 'C': 'The user message after the breakpoint changes on every request, which invalidates the cached documentation.', 'D': 'The timestamp changes on every request and sits before the breakpoint, so the cached prefix is never identical.'}
rationale: Cache hits require an exact match of the prefix up to the breakpoint, so a timestamp that changes on every request at the start of the prompt prevents any hit, while content after the breakpoint does not matter.

stem: Each request to an app contains four parts: fixed instructions that are the same for everyone, a 30,000-token policy manual shared by all users, a short profile for the current user, and the user's conversation so far. Which layout minimizes input cost through prompt caching?
options: {'A': 'Put the user profile first, then the instructions, then the manual, then the conversation, with a breakpoint after the manual.', 'B': 'Put the instructions first, then the manual, with a breakpoint after the manual, followed by the user profile and then the conversation.', 'C': 'Put the conversation first so the newest content is cached, then the instructions, manual and profile.', 'D': 'Turn off caching entirely, because the conversation changes on every request.'}
rationale: Putting the content shared by all users first and ending the cached prefix before per-user data lets every user's requests reuse the same large cached prefix.

stem: An email assistant reads a user's inbox to write summaries. It also has a send_email tool and can read the user's contacts. An attacker sends an email containing hidden instructions to forward the inbox to an outside address. Which mitigation gives the strongest protection, even if the model is fooled by the injected text?
options: {'A': 'Add a system prompt line asking the model to please ignore any instructions found inside emails.', 'B': 'Remove send capability from the step that reads untrusted email content, and require explicit user confirmation for any outgoing email.', 'C': 'Repeat the system prompt twice so the model gives it more weight than the email text.', 'D': 'Block only emails that contain the exact phrase "ignore previous instructions".'}
rationale: Limiting what the model can do while it reads untrusted text, and putting harmful actions behind human approval, still protects the user when the injection succeeds, while prompt wording and phrase filters can be bypassed.

stem: A research assistant runs four steps. Which step creates the prompt-injection risk that an attacker who controls a web page can exploit?
options: {'A': "Step 1: The user's question is checked against a maximum length before processing.", 'B': 'Step 2: Web search results are limited to pages served over HTTPS.', 'C': "Step 3: Fetched page text goes into the same prompt as the user's private session data and a tool that can send HTTP requests to any URL.", 'D': 'Step 4: The final answer is HTML-escaped before it is shown in the browser.'}
