rationale: Putting attacker-controlled text in front of a model that holds private data and can reach any URL lets injected instructions send that data out.

stem: A team wants to know whether prompt version 2 of their support bot gives better answers than version 1, using a method free from data leakage and judging bias. Which evaluation method is valid?
options: {'A': 'Score both versions on the 100 examples the team used while writing version 2, since those examples are already well understood.', 'B': 'Ask an LLM judge to rate each answer, telling it which answers came from the new prompt so it knows what to look for.', 'C': 'Treat the version with longer average answers as better, since longer answers always contain more helpful detail.', 'D': 'Use a held-out set of representative real queries and blind pairwise judging in random order, with the judge checked against human ratings.'}
rationale: Held-out representative data, blinding, random order and a judge checked against humans together remove data leakage, labelling bias, position bias and an unverified judge.

stem: An engineer reports that a new prompt raised accuracy from 81% to 94% on a 200-question test set. You learn that these 200 questions are the same ones the engineer used to repeatedly test and adjust the new prompt during development. What is the main flaw in this result?
options: {'A': 'The prompt was tuned on the test questions, so the score overstates how well it will do on new questions.', 'B': 'Accuracy can never be used as a metric for language model outputs.', 'C': 'Any test set with fewer than 10,000 questions produces meaningless results.', 'D': 'A baseline of 81% is too high for any prompt change to improve on it.'}
rationale: Adjusting the prompt on the very questions used for scoring overfits it to them, so the improvement may not carry over to unseen inputs.

stem: A legal tool must answer questions about a 2,000-page set of contracts, which is far larger than the model's context window. Answers must quote exact clauses word for word, and many clauses refer to other numbered sections. Which strategy fits best?
options: {'A': 'Cut the contracts down to the first part that fits in the context window and answer from that text.', 'B': 'Summarize the contracts in rounds until the summary fits, then quote clauses from the summary.', 'C': 'Split the contracts along section boundaries, retrieve the sections relevant to each question along with the sections they reference, and quote from the retrieved text.', 'D': 'Raise the maximum output token limit so the model can read the full contract set in a single call.'}
rationale: Retrieval that follows section structure and cross-references keeps the exact clause wording within the window, while truncation drops content, summaries lose the original wording, and output limits do not increase input capacity.

stem: An app places the user's question at the very top of the prompt, followed by about 150,000 tokens of documents. With short document sets the answers are reliable. With long ones, answers are accurate when the relevant fact appears near the start or end of the documents but often miss facts located in the middle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: {'A': 'The max_tokens setting is too low, so the answers are cut off before the facts appear.', 'B': 'The model attends less reliably to the middle of very long contexts, and putting the question before the documents makes this worse.', 'C': 'The sampling temperature is too high, which causes random errors that have nothing to do with position.', 'D': 'The tokenizer deletes tokens from the middle of any input longer than 100,000 tokens.'}
rationale: Models recall content in the middle of long contexts less reliably, and placing the question after the documents or extracting relevant passages first reduces this loss.

stem: Lane North sends a 4 MB payload by ferry to lane South once per beat. South has three tiles and runs for four beats with ferry.eager enabled. Which result follows from this configuration?
options: {'A': 'South has a billing weight of 12, and the payload is automatically restored to its original order.', 'B': 'North has a billing weight of 24, and the payload arrives as one unit on every fifth beat.', 'C': "South has a billing weight of 24, and the payload's shards may be delivered in the wrong order.", 'D': 'South has a billing weight of 48 because both ferry size and eager mode double its weight.'}
rationale: The 4 MB payload is sharded and not reordered, while eager mode doubles South's normal weight of three tiles times four beats from 12 to 24.

stem: A ferry carrying a 1.8 MB message consistently delivers the message intact, but the receiving tile incorrectly processes fields in reverse order. Which diagnosis is best supported by the Tessellate rules?
options: {'A': 'The ferry must have sharded the message because all ferry payloads can arrive out of order.', 'B': 'The problem is not explained by ferry sharding, because payloads are split only when larger than 2 MB.', 'C': 'The ferry reordered the message because eager mode always reverses field order.', 'D': 'The message was reordered because ferries copy data only once per beat.'}
rationale: At 1.8 MB, the message is below the threshold for ferry sharding, so the documented out-of-order shard behavior does not explain the reversal.

stem: An unpinned lane contains a tile whose retry.limit is 7. The tile fails after receiving input X, and upstream later changes the value to Y. Which behavior should the operator expect during retries and after a final failure?
options: {'A': 'Retries occur immediately using X, and a final failure fails only that lane.', 'B': 'Retries use Y with exponential back-off, and a final failure fails the whole run.', 'C': "Retries occur immediately using Y, and a final failure removes the lane's pin.", 'D': 'Retries use X with back-off, and a final failure fails the whole run.'}
rationale: A retry limit above 5 disables back-off, retries retain original input X, and failure in an unpinned lane affects only that lane.

stem: A payment tile failed with an outdated account balance. The balance has since been updated, but another retry would still use the outdated value. Which action addresses the stale-input problem?
options: {'A': "Renew the lane's pin before the next retry.", 'B': 'Raise retry.limit above 5 to force an input refresh.', 'C': 'Start a new execution of the tile using the updated upstream state instead of retrying the failed execution.', 'D': 'Enable tracing so the retry substitutes the latest recorded input.'}
rationale: Retries always reuse the original inputs, so only a new execution can acquire the updated upstream value.

stem: A lane named _settlement contains three tiles and must run on every beat both before and after a planned Tessellate upgrade. Which operating plan meets the requirement?
options: {'A': 'Pin the lane once before the upgrade; upgrades preserve active pins for 12 more beats.', 'B': 'Leave the lane unpinned during the upgrade because underscore lanes automatically run after upgrades.', 'C': 'Add a fourth watchdog tile to the pinned lane so it can restore the pin after the upgrade.', 'D': 'Pin the lane before the upgrade, pin it again after the upgrade, and renew the new pin every 12 beats as needed.'}
rationale: The underscore lane requires a pin, upgrading resets that pin, and each replacement pin expires after 12 beats unless renewed.

stem: A visible lane was pinned to run every beat. Immediately after Tessellate was upgraded, the lane no longer runs on every beat even though fewer than 12 beats have passed since pinning. What should the operator check first?
options: {'A': "Whether the upgrade reset the lane's pin.", 'B': "Whether the lane's ledger was compacted.", 'C': 'Whether the lane received a payload larger than 2 MB.', 'D': 'Whether an eighth tile was rejected from the lane.'}
rationale: Every Tessellate upgrade resets all pins, regardless of how recently they were created.

stem: Two separate lanes are each half full and repeatedly run during the same beats. Which change is specified to reduce their billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Split each lane into two smaller lanes.', 'B': 'Merge the two half-full lanes into one lane.', 'C': 'Run ledger.compact on both lanes after every beat.', 'D': 'Retain both lanes but delete their stored ledger history.'}
rationale: Tessellate explicitly reduces billing weight when two half-full lanes are merged, whereas splitting and ledger compaction do not provide that reduction.

stem: A lane has six tiles, but only two perform useful work during each of ten beats. An operator predicts a billing weight of 20 because the other four tiles are idle. What is wrong with this prediction?
options: {'A': 'Billing is based only on ferry payload size, not tiles or beats.', 'B': 'Every idle tile counts twice even when eager mode is disabled.', 'C': 'All six tiles count while the lane runs, so the billing weight is 60 before any eager multiplier.', 'D': 'Only pinned tiles count, so the billing weight is actually zero.'}
rationale: Idle tiles in a running lane still count, making the weight six tiles times ten beats, or 60.

stem: A lane contains seven active tiles when two more tiles are submitted to it. What does Tessellate do with the newly submitted tiles?
options: {'A': 'It silently queues both because the lane is already at its seven-tile capacity.', 'B': 'It rejects both with capacity errors.', 'C': 'It runs one as an eighth tile and queues only the ninth.', 'D': "It moves both into a new lane that shares the original lane's memory."}
rationale: Once a lane has seven tiles, additional tiles are silently queued rather than rejected or moved.

stem: Eight tiles must all run, and tiles placed in different lanes must exchange results using a supported Tessellate mechanism. Which layout is valid?
options: {'A': 'Place all eight in one ordinary lane so they can use shared memory simultaneously.', 'B': 'Place four tiles in each of two ordinary lanes and connect the lanes with a ferry.', 'C': "Place four tiles in each of two ordinary lanes and let them directly read each other's lane memory.", 'D': 'Place all eight in one pinned lane to increase its capacity beyond seven.'}
rationale: Eight running tiles require more than one lane, and a ferry is the only supported way for tiles in different lanes to exchange data.

stem: A 3 MB ferry sends data from lane Alpha to lane Beta with ferry.eager set to true. Beta contains four tiles and runs for five beats. Which result follows from the ferry size and eager setting?
options: {'A': "The payload is sharded and automatically reordered, and Alpha's billing weight is doubled.", 'B': "The payload is sharded and may arrive out of order, and Beta's billing weight is doubled from 20 to 40.", 'C': "The payload remains unsharded because ferry size does not affect delivery, and Beta's billing weight is 20.", 'D': "The payload is delivered continuously rather than once per beat, and only Beta's active tiles are billed."}
rationale: A ferry larger than 2 MB is sharded without automatic reordering, and eager mode doubles the receiving lane's weight from four tiles times five beats to 40.

stem: A 2.6 MB file crosses a ferry, and the receiving lane occasionally reads the file's final section before its first section. No retries occurred. What best explains the problem?
options: {'A': 'Ferries larger than 2 MB are split into shards that may arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not reorder them.', 'B': 'The ferry alphabetically sorts all sections larger than 2 MB before delivery.', 'C': 'The receiving lane reverses ferry data whenever it contains an idle tile.', 'D': 'Metrics sampling on every fifth beat changes the order of the delivered data.'}
rationale: A payload over 2 MB is sharded, its shards may arrive out of order, and Tessellate performs no reordering.

stem: A tile in a pinned lane starts with input version 1 and fails. Upstream then changes the input to version 2. The tile has retry.limit set to 6 and continues to fail. Which sequence should the operator expect?
options: {'A': 'The retries use version 2 with increasing back-off, and only the tile is removed.', 'B': 'The retries use version 1 with normal back-off, and the pinned lane becomes unpinned.', 'C': 'The retries use version 2 immediately, and only the lane fails after the final attempt.', 'D': 'The retries use version 1 with no back-off, and the whole run fails if the tile remains failed.'}
rationale: Retries preserve the original version 1 inputs, a retry limit above 5 disables back-off, and failure in a pinned lane fails the whole run.

stem: A failed tile is waiting to retry, but its original input is now stale because upstream data has been corrected. The next attempt must use the corrected data. What should the operator do?
options: {'A': 'Raise retry.limit above 5 so the retry refreshes its inputs.', 'B': 'Start a fresh tile execution after the upstream correction instead of continuing the old retry sequence.', 'C': 'Enable trace so the retry substitutes the newest upstream value.', 'D': 'Run ledger.compact so the retry forgets its original input.'}
rationale: Retries always reuse the original inputs, so only a fresh execution can take the corrected upstream value.

stem: Four audit tiles must use underscore-prefixed lane names and run on every beat for 30 beats. Which configuration meets both the execution and capacity rules?
options: {'A': 'Put all four tiles in one pinned underscore lane and renew the pin once after beat 12.', 'B': 'Put all four tiles in one unpinned underscore lane because underscore lanes run automatically.', 'C': 'Split the tiles between two pinned underscore lanes with no more than three tiles per lane, renewing each pin before every 12-beat expiry.', 'D': 'Split the tiles between two unpinned underscore lanes and enable ferry.eager.'}
rationale: Underscore lanes require pins to run, pinned lanes can contain at most three tiles, and pins must be renewed before they expire after 12 beats.

stem: A pinned lane named _audit ran on every beat and then stopped immediately after its twelfth beat. There was no upgrade, failure, or capacity change. What should the operator check first?
options: {'A': 'Whether the pin expired because pin.renew was not used.', 'B': "Whether ledger.compact deleted the lane's execution permission.", 'C': 'Whether the scheduler permanently rejects every underscore lane after 12 beats.', 'D': 'Whether the lane reached the normal seven-tile limit and was automatically erased.'}
rationale: Pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed, and an underscore lane stops running when it no longer has a pin.

stem: Two separate lanes each contain three tiles and run for ten beats, producing a combined billing weight of 60. All six tiles can operate in one ordinary lane without ferries or pinning. Which change is specified to reduce billing weight?
options: {'A': 'Merge the two half-full lanes into one lane.', 'B': 'Split each lane into three one-tile lanes.', 'C': 'Run ledger.compact while leaving both lanes unchanged.', 'D': 'Retain both lanes but delete their stored billing history.'}
rationale: Tessellate explicitly states that merging two half-full lanes reduces billing weight, while splitting or compacting the ledger does not.

stem: A lane contains five tiles, but only two are actively working during each of six running beats. An operator calculates its billing weight as 12 because the three idle tiles should not count. What is wrong with this calculation?
options: {'A': 'Billing is based only on ferry payload size, not tiles or beats.', 'B': 'Each active tile counts twice even when ferry.eager is false.', 'C': 'Idle tiles in a running lane still count, so the weight is five tiles times six beats, or 30.', 'D': 'Billing weight is always seven tiles times the number of beats, regardless of lane contents.'}
rationale: All tiles in a running lane count, including idle ones, so five tiles over six beats produce a billing weight of 30.

stem: An ordinary lane already contains seven tiles when an operator submits an eighth tile to that lane. What does Tessellate do?
options: {'A': 'It rejects the entire lane and fails the run.', 'B': 'It silently queues the eighth tile instead of rejecting it.', 'C': 'It automatically moves the oldest tile into a new lane.', 'D': 'It runs all eight tiles but doubles their billing weight.'}
rationale: A lane's active capacity is seven tiles, and an eighth tile is silently queued rather than rejected.

stem: Six tiles need immediate shared-memory access to one another's data. The layout must not use ferries, pins, or underscore lanes. Which design satisfies the requirement?
options: {'A': 'Place three tiles in each of two ordinary lanes because all ordinary lanes share memory.', 'B': 'Place each tile in its own lane and rely on metrics sampling to transfer data.', 'C': 'Place the six tiles in one underscore lane so the scheduler can run them automatically.', 'D': 'Place all six tiles in one ordinary unpinned lane, which is within the seven-tile capacity.'}
rationale: Tiles share memory only within the same lane, and six tiles fit in one ordinary lane without requiring a pin.

stem: A 3 MB ferry transfers data from lane Source to lane Report once per beat. The ferry has eager mode enabled, and Report contains four tiles that run for five beats. Which result follows from this configuration?
options: {'A': 'The payload is divided into shards that Tessellate automatically reorders, and Report has a billing weight of 20.', 'B': 'The payload is divided into shards that may arrive out of order, and Report has a billing weight of 40.', 'C': 'The payload is transferred continuously without sharding, and Source has a billing weight of 40.', 'D': 'The payload is rejected for exceeding 2 MB, so neither lane receives any billing weight.'}
rationale: A ferry over 2 MB is sharded without automatic reordering, and eager mode doubles Report's normal weight of four tiles times five beats from 20 to 40.

stem: A lane receives a 2.8 MB serialized document through a ferry. Logs show that all parts arrive, but some later parts appear before earlier parts. Which diagnosis best matches Tessellate's ferry behavior?
options: {'A': 'The document was split into shards, which may arrive out of order because Tessellate does not reorder them.', 'B': "The document exceeded the lane's seven-tile capacity, so Tessellate reversed its parts.", 'C': 'Eager mode always sorts ferry data in descending order.', 'D': 'The ferry transmitted the document only once because ferries do not operate on beats.'}
rationale: Payloads larger than 2 MB are split into shards that may arrive out of order, and Tessellate does not restore their order.

stem: A tile in a pinned lane starts with input version 1 and fails. Upstream data then changes to version 2. The tile has retry.limit set to 6 and continues failing through all allowed attempts. Which behavior should the operator expect?
options: {'A': 'The retries use version 2 with increasing back-off, and only the tile is affected at the end.', 'B': 'The retries use version 1 with no back-off, and the whole run fails if the tile remains failed.', 'C': 'The retries use version 2 with no back-off, and the failed lane is automatically unpinned.', 'D': 'The retries alternate between both input versions, and the whole run succeeds after the sixth attempt.'}
rationale: Retries reuse the original version 1 input, a retry limit above 5 disables back-off, and failure in a pinned lane fails the whole run.

stem: A tile failed while using an incorrect upstream value. The upstream value has now been corrected, but the tile's pending retries still use the old value. Which action ensures that the corrected value is used?
options: {'A': 'Increase retry.limit above 5 so the retries refresh their inputs.', 'B': 'Run ledger.compact before the next retry.', 'C': 'End the existing retry sequence and start a fresh tile execution after the upstream correction.', 'D': 'Pin the lane so retries inherit the newest upstream input.'}
rationale: Retries always reuse the original inputs, so a fresh execution is required to read the corrected upstream value.

stem: Four audit tiles must run on every beat for 30 beats. Policy requires their lane names to begin with an underscore. Which setup meets all of these requirements?
options: {'A': 'Place all four tiles in one pinned underscore lane and allow its pin to expire normally.', 'B': 'Place all four tiles in one unpinned underscore lane because underscore lanes run automatically.', 'C': 'Split the tiles between two pinned underscore lanes with no more than three tiles per lane, and renew both pins before each expiration.', 'D': 'Place the tiles in two unpinned underscore lanes and enable eager ferries between them.'}
rationale: Underscore lanes require pins to run, pinned lanes are capped at three tiles, and pins must be renewed because they expire after 12 beats.

stem: The pinned lane _audit ran on every beat for 12 beats and then stopped. It has only two tiles, and Tessellate was not upgraded. Which explanation is most likely?
options: {'A': 'The lane exceeded the three-tile limit for pinned lanes.', 'B': 'Its pin expired because pin.renew was not used.', 'C': 'Underscore lanes are deleted automatically after 12 beats.', 'D': 'The scheduler moved the lane into an eighth-tile queue.'}
rationale: Pins expire after 12 beats unless renewed, and an underscore lane stops running when it is no longer pinned.

stem: A receiving lane contains four tiles and runs for five beats with ferry.eager enabled, producing a billing weight of 40. The workload and number of beats cannot change. Which change reduces its billing weight to 20?
options: {'A': 'Disable ferry.eager for the ferry feeding the lane.', 'B': 'Run ledger.compact after the fifth beat.', 'C': 'Mark two of the four tiles as idle while leaving them in the running lane.', 'D': 'Split the lane into two lanes while leaving eager mode enabled.'}
rationale: Without eager mode, the lane's billing weight is four tiles times five beats, or 20, whereas compaction and idleness do not remove billed tiles.

stem: During a cost review, four operators make statements about Tessellate billing. Which statement reflects a mistaken assumption?
options: {'A': 'Idle tiles in a lane still count while that lane is running.', 'B': 'An eager ferry doubles the billing weight of the tiles in its receiving lane.', 'C': 'Running ledger.compact lowers future billing weight because it removes stored history.', 'D': 'Merging two half-full lanes into one lane reduces billing weight.'}
rationale: ledger.compact reduces stored history only and has no effect on billing weight.

stem: A normal lane currently contains the maximum of seven tiles. An operator submits an eighth tile to that same lane and sees no error. What has Tessellate done with the new tile?
options: {'A': 'It silently queued the eighth tile.', 'B': 'It discarded the oldest tile and inserted the new one.', 'C': 'It automatically created and pinned a second lane.', 'D': 'It began running all eight tiles despite the stated limit.'}
rationale: When a lane already has seven tiles, an eighth tile is silently queued rather than rejected.

stem: Six tiles must exchange data through shared memory with no ferry transfer, and they must run in a scheduler-visible layout that does not require pin renewal. Which design satisfies the requirement?
options: {'A': 'Put three tiles in each of two ordinary unpinned lanes because different lanes automatically share memory.', 'B': 'Put all six tiles in one ordinary, non-underscore, unpinned lane.', 'C': 'Put all six tiles in one pinned lane, even though pinned lanes allow seven tiles.', 'D': 'Put all six tiles in one unpinned underscore lane so the scheduler runs it automatically.'}
rationale: Six tiles fit in one ordinary lane, tiles in the same lane share memory, and a non-underscore lane does not need a pin to be scheduler-visible.

stem: In Tessellate 4, an operator sets ferry.eager = true on a ferry that sends a 3 MB payload into a receiving lane. The receiving lane has 4 tiles, and the operator expects it to run for 10 beats. With eager off, that lane's billing weight would be 4 × 10 = 40. What should the operator expect?
options: {'A': "The receiving lane's weight becomes 80, and the payload's pieces may arrive out of order and stay that way.", 'B': "The receiving lane stays at 40 while the sending lane's weight doubles, and the pieces may arrive out of order and stay that way.", 'C': "The receiving lane's weight becomes 80, and Tessellate puts the payload's pieces back in order before delivery.", 'D': "The receiving lane stays at 40 while the sending lane's weight doubles, and Tessellate puts the pieces back in order before delivery."}
rationale: Eager ferries double the billing weight of every tile in the receiving lane, and payloads over 2 MB are split into shards that Tessellate does not reorder.

stem: A travel agent uses a book_flight tool. When the tool times out after submitting a reservation, the agent retries and sometimes purchases the same itinerary twice. Which tool-design change is the best fix?
options: {'A': 'The tool should accept an idempotency key for each intended booking and return the existing result when that key is retried.', 'B': 'The tool description should tell the model not to retry requests that take longer than expected.', 'C': 'The agent should use a higher temperature so that it varies its response after a timeout.', 'D': 'The tool should return shorter error messages to reduce the number of tokens in the conversation.'}
rationale: A server-enforced idempotency key makes retries safe even when the agent cannot tell whether the original booking succeeded.

stem: An agent can call get_order_status with an order number or list_recent_orders with a customer ID. Users usually ask, “Where is my latest order?” The agent repeatedly calls get_order_status with the words “latest order,” which fail schema validation. Both tools have accurate parameter types, but only one-line descriptions. What most likely causes this misuse?
options: {'A': 'The model cannot use identifiers returned by one tool as inputs to another tool.', 'B': 'Schema validation prevents the model from reasoning about relative dates such as “latest.”', 'C': "The tool guidance does not explain that the agent must first list the customer's orders to resolve a relative reference before requesting a specific order's status.", 'D': 'The status tool needs to return tracking events in chronological order.'}
rationale: The missing workflow and prerequisite guidance leaves the model unaware that it must resolve “latest” to an order number before calling the status tool.

stem: An application expects prompt-cache hits because its system instructions and tool definitions are logically unchanged. However, it rebuilds the tool-definition JSON for every request from an unordered collection, so property and tool order sometimes differ. The changing user message is appended afterward. Why are cache hits inconsistent?
options: {'A': 'Prompt caches generally refuse to cache any prefix containing JSON schemas.', 'B': 'The changing serialization alters the prefix token sequence even though the tools are semantically equivalent.', 'C': 'A cached prefix can be reused only when the generated answer is also identical.', 'D': 'Tool definitions must appear after the user message to become cacheable.'}
rationale: Prefix caches depend on identical serialized tokens, so nondeterministic ordering can prevent reuse of semantically unchanged content.

stem: A service handles requests for many organizations. All requests share a large policy manual, each organization has a stable configuration block, and each individual request has changing case details. Which ordering best supports cost-saving prefix caching?
options: {'A': 'The prompt should begin with case details, then include the organization configuration and finally the shared manual.', 'B': 'The prompt should alternate paragraphs from the manual with changing case details.', 'C': 'The prompt should place organization configuration first, changing case details second, and the shared manual last.', 'D': 'The prompt should place the shared manual first, the organization configuration second, and changing case details last.'}
rationale: Ordering content from most widely stable to most request-specific allows requests to share the longest applicable cached prefixes.

stem: An email assistant reads untrusted messages and can draft replies, search private mail, and send messages. The product must prevent a malicious email from causing private messages to be forwarded to an attacker while still allowing ordinary sending. Which control is strongest?
options: {'A': 'The application should hide tool names from the email text before giving the text to the model.', 'B': 'The system prompt should include several examples of refusing requests found inside emails.', 'C': 'A policy-enforcing broker should block sensitive-content transfers to unapproved recipients and require explicit user authorization for newly introduced recipients before executing a send.', 'D': 'A second model should rewrite every incoming email into a friendlier tone before the assistant reads it.'}
rationale: An external broker that enforces recipient and data-transfer policy prevents exfiltration even if malicious content controls the model's proposed action.

stem: A document-processing service lets users upload files. A model reads each file, chooses a storage destination, and emits a move_file tool call. The application automatically executes every syntactically valid call using a service account that can access all departments. Which step is directly exploitable through prompt injection in an uploaded file?
options: {'A': 'The service converts uploaded files to text before sending them to the model.', 'B': 'The application executes model-selected destinations with broad service-account privileges without an independent authorization check.', 'C': 'The move_file tool returns a confirmation message after moving a file.', 'D': 'The application records uploaded filenames in an audit log.'}
rationale: Automatically executing model-directed actions with excessive privileges lets instructions embedded in untrusted files cross the authorization boundary.

stem: A team is comparing two agents that resolve data-analysis tasks by writing and running code. Tasks vary greatly in difficulty, execution can be nondeterministic, and some outputs look plausible despite containing wrong numbers. Which evaluation design provides the strongest comparison?
options: {'A': 'The team should compare average response length across all tasks because more detailed analyses are usually more accurate.', 'B': 'The team should let each agent select the tasks on which it expects to perform best and compare its selected-task accuracy.', 'C': 'The team should have one developer inspect a single run from each agent while knowing which system produced it.', 'D': 'The team should run both agents repeatedly on the same representative held-out tasks, verify numerical results with task-specific executable checks, compare paired outcomes by difficulty group, and quantify uncertainty.'}
rationale: Paired repeated testing with executable correctness checks, representative held-out tasks, stratification, and uncertainty accounts for both task variation and nondeterminism.

stem: An agent is evaluated on 1,000 requests. The report claims 96% accuracy, but the calculation includes only the 720 requests for which the agent returned a final answer and excludes all timeouts, crashes, and abandoned tool runs. What is the main flaw?
options: {'A': 'The reported accuracy has survivorship bias because operational failures were omitted from the denominator.', 'B': 'Accuracy cannot be used for any evaluation containing more than 500 requests.', 'C': 'Timeouts should be counted as correct whenever the agent began the right tool call.', 'D': 'The evaluation is invalid because every request should have a unique scoring metric.'}
rationale: Excluding requests that failed to complete inflates the apparent end-to-end success rate.

stem: An engineering assistant must answer questions that may require tracing a configuration value from a deployment file through several functions in a codebase too large for one context window. Which strategy is best?
options: {'A': 'The application should truncate every source file to its first 200 lines and send all truncated files together.', 'B': 'The application should summarize the entire repository once and answer exclusively from that summary.', 'C': 'The application should retrieve likely entry points, follow symbol definitions, references, imports, and configuration dependencies iteratively, then provide the model with the relevant code slices and file locations.', 'D': 'The application should sort files alphabetically and fill the context window until no tokens remain.'}
rationale: Iterative dependency-aware retrieval preserves the exact code path needed for multi-hop reasoning without loading the entire repository.

stem: A chat application limits each request to a fixed input-token budget by deleting the oldest messages before calling the model. In long conversations, the assistant suddenly forgets a constraint the user specified near the beginning, although recent turns remain coherent. What is the most likely explanation?
options: {'A': "The model's output temperature automatically rises as conversations become longer.", 'B': 'The assistant can remember constraints only when they appear in a system message.', 'C': 'The tokenizer has converted the early constraint into an unsupported character encoding.', 'D': "The application's truncation policy removed the message containing the constraint without preserving it in a summary or structured state."}
rationale: Dropping the oldest turns can silently remove still-relevant requirements unless they are retained separately or summarized.

stem: A 3 MB ferry sends data to lane Beta with ferry.eager set to true. Beta contains four tiles and runs for five beats. Which result should the operator expect?
options: {'A': 'The data is sharded and restored to sending order, and Beta has a billing weight of 40.', 'B': 'The data is sharded with no guaranteed arrival order, and Beta has a billing weight of 40.', 'C': 'The data is sharded with no guaranteed arrival order, and Beta has a billing weight of 20.', 'D': 'The data is transferred as one unit in sending order, and Beta has a billing weight of 20.'}
rationale: A ferry over 2 MB is split into shards without automatic reordering, and eager mode doubles Beta's ordinary weight of four tiles times five beats to 40.

stem: An agent has a lookup_customer tool that requires an exact customer ID and a search_customers tool that accepts a name or partial email address. Both tools are described only as “Find a customer,” and the agent frequently sends names to lookup_customer. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The overlapping descriptions fail to explain the distinct use cases and input requirements of the tools.', 'B': 'The model cannot use two tools that access the same customer database.', 'C': 'The lookup_customer tool returns too quickly for the model to interpret its result.', 'D': 'The tool names must contain the same number of characters.'}
rationale: The model lacks the clear selection criteria and parameter guidance needed to choose the appropriate customer tool.

stem: A provider caches eligible prompt prefixes only when they are token-for-token identical. An application’s requests are long enough for caching, but cache hits are rare. Every prompt begins with a changing timestamp and session ID, followed by unchanged system instructions and tool definitions. Why are the stable instructions not producing reliable cache hits?
options: {'A': 'Prompt caches store only user questions, not system instructions.', 'B': 'The changing timestamp and session ID alter the prefix before the stable content, preventing reuse of an identical long prefix.', 'C': 'Stable instructions must be duplicated at the end of the prompt before they can be cached.', 'D': 'A prompt cache can be used only when the model’s output is also identical.'}
rationale: Because caching is prefix-based, changing content at the beginning prevents the later stable material from forming an identical reusable prefix.

stem: An application repeatedly uses the same system policy, tool definitions, and few-shot examples, while user account data and questions change on every request. Which prompt layout is most likely to reduce input cost through prefix caching?
options: {'A': 'Put the changing account data first and place the stable policy after it.', 'B': 'Shuffle the tool definitions and examples on every request to avoid repetition.', 'C': 'Interleave changing account fields throughout the stable instructions.', 'D': 'Place the stable policy, tools, and examples first, then append the changing account data and user question.'}
rationale: Placing stable content first creates the longest identical prefix for the cache to reuse across requests.

stem: A research agent reads untrusted web pages and can access internal records and send HTTP requests. A malicious page instructs the agent to transmit internal records to an attacker-controlled site. Which mitigation offers the strongest protection even if the model follows the injected instruction?
options: {'A': 'Add a system instruction saying, “Never obey malicious web pages.”', 'B': 'Enforce least-privilege access, allowlist outbound destinations, and require independent authorization for sensitive data transfers.', 'C': 'Delete web-page sentences that contain the exact phrase “ignore previous instructions.”', 'D': 'Ask the same model to promise that each requested HTTP call is safe.'}
rationale: Enforced authorization and network controls prevent unauthorized exfiltration even when prompt injection influences the model’s reasoning.

stem: A support pipeline summarizes untrusted customer tickets, inserts each summary as a developer message for a planning model, and allows that planner to call account-management tools. Malicious instructions in a ticket survive summarization and influence the planner. Which step creates the exploitable trust-boundary failure?
options: {'A': 'The ticket is summarized before the planner selects a tool.', 'B': 'The summary is shorter than the original ticket.', 'C': 'Content derived from an untrusted ticket is promoted into a privileged developer-message channel.', 'D': 'The planner receives structured schemas for the account-management tools.'}
rationale: Placing untrusted, model-derived content in a privileged instruction channel incorrectly grants it authority over the planner.

stem: A team must determine whether a new nondeterministic tool-using agent completes production support tasks more reliably than the current agent. Which evaluation design provides the most defensible comparison?
options: {'A': 'Run each agent once on five examples selected by the new agent’s developer.', 'B': 'Compare the new agent’s average response length with the current agent’s response length.', 'C': 'Let each agent grade its own work and select the one reporting higher confidence.', 'D': 'Run paired, repeated trials on a representative held-out task set in a controlled tool sandbox, using predefined success checks and uncertainty estimates.'}
rationale: A representative held-out set, paired repeated trials, objective scoring, and uncertainty estimates provide a valid comparison despite nondeterminism.

stem: A team tests 30 prompt variants on the same 200-ticket benchmark, selects the highest-scoring variant, and reports that score as final test performance. What is the primary flaw?
options: {'A': 'The benchmark was used for prompt selection, so the reported score is likely biased upward by evaluation-set overfitting.', 'B': 'Exactly 30 prompt variants are required to be evaluated on 30 different model providers.', 'C': 'Prompt evaluation is valid only when every response contains the same number of words.', 'D': 'The team should always choose the first prompt tested rather than the highest-scoring prompt.'}
rationale: Selecting the best prompt on the benchmark turns that benchmark into tuning data, so an untouched test set is needed for final evaluation.

stem: A contract-analysis application must answer questions about rare clauses and cross-references across documents that cannot all fit in the model’s context window. Which strategy best preserves relevant source detail while controlling prompt size?
options: {'A': 'Include only the first page of each contract because legal documents state all important terms at the beginning.', 'B': 'Replace every contract with a single two-sentence summary and permanently discard the source sections.', 'C': 'Use section-aware retrieval, decompose the question, rerank candidate passages, and include neighboring or cross-referenced sections with citations.', 'D': 'Truncate all contracts at the same character position without considering their structure.'}
rationale: Structured retrieval and cross-reference expansion bring the most relevant detailed evidence into the limited context while preserving traceability.

stem: An assistant becomes less accurate as conversations grow, although the prompt remains slightly below the model’s advertised context limit. Logs show the full chat history, duplicated retrieval passages, and important instructions buried near the middle. What is the best diagnosis?
options: {'A': 'Models process only the first half of any prompt, regardless of context-window size.', 'B': 'Duplicated and irrelevant context is distracting the model, and buried information may suffer from middle-position retrieval weakness.', 'C': 'Retrieved passages cannot legally appear in the same prompt as chat history.', 'D': 'The model needs more output tokens because output length determines how much input it can read.'}

stem: A purchasing agent can call submit_order, which immediately places an order. When a request omits the quantity, the agent sometimes guesses and submits an expensive order. Which tool-design change best prevents this failure without removing automation?
options: {'A': 'The application should raise the model temperature so it explores more possible quantities.', 'B': 'The tool should use the value zero whenever the quantity is missing.', 'C': 'The application should separate order preparation from execution, validate all required fields, and require confirmation of the exact order before submission.', 'D': 'The tool description should tell the model to make its best guess when information is missing.'}
rationale: A validated prepare-and-confirm flow prevents the agent from executing an irreversible action with guessed or missing parameters.

stem: An agent has get_invoice, which requires an exact invoice ID, and search_invoices, which accepts a supplier name or date range. Both tools are described only as tools that find invoices, and the agent often sends supplier names to get_invoice. What is the most likely cause?
options: {'A': 'The tool descriptions fail to distinguish their use cases and required input formats.', 'B': 'The agent cannot use two tools that operate on the same type of business record.', 'C': 'The get_invoice tool returns invoice details too quickly for the model to interpret them.', 'D': 'The agent needs a larger maximum output-token limit before it can select a tool.'}
rationale: Overlapping descriptions that omit selection criteria and input constraints make it difficult for the model to choose the correct tool.

stem: A provider caches only prompt prefixes that are identical token for token. rationale: Variable content at the beginning prevents the later stable material from forming an identical reusable prefix.

stem: An application sends the same system instructions, tool definitions, and examples on thousands of requests, but each request has different customer data and a different question. Which layout best reduces cost with prefix-based prompt caching?
options: {'A': 'The application should put the changing customer data first and the stable instructions last.', 'B': 'The application should alternate the order of tools on every request to distribute cache usage.', 'C': 'The application should mix customer data into each example so every section contains current information.', 'D': 'The application should put stable instructions, tools, and examples first, then append customer data and the question.'}
rationale: Placing shared content in a stable prefix maximizes the number of reusable cached tokens.

stem: An agent reads untrusted web pages and can access confidential company records through tools. A page contains hidden instructions telling the agent to send those records to an attacker. Which mitigation offers the strongest protection?
options: {'A': 'The application should add a bold system instruction saying that malicious pages must be ignored.', 'B': 'The application should enforce least-privilege permissions, block unauthorized outbound destinations, and require approval for sensitive transfers outside the model.', 'C': "The application should remove the exact phrase 'ignore previous instructions' from every page.", 'D': 'The application should ask the same model to confirm that a proposed transfer is safe.'}
rationale: External authorization and capability controls prevent unauthorized disclosure even if the model follows injected instructions.

stem: A pipeline summarizes untrusted customer messages and inserts each summary as a developer message for a second model that can suspend accounts. Malicious instructions in a customer message survive summarization and cause an account suspension. Which step creates the key vulnerability?
options: {'A': 'The first model summarizes the message instead of translating it.', 'B': 'The second model receives a description of the account-suspension tool.', 'C': 'The pipeline promotes content derived from an untrusted message into a privileged developer-message channel.', 'D': 'The pipeline uses two models rather than one model.'}
rationale: Promoting untrusted derived content into a privileged instruction channel creates an exploitable trust-boundary failure.

stem: A team must compare a new nondeterministic tool-using agent with the current agent on production-like support tasks. Which evaluation design provides the most credible evidence of improvement?

rationale: A representative held-out set, controlled paired trials, objective scoring, repetition, and uncertainty produce a defensible comparison.

stem: A legal assistant must answer questions about rare clauses and cross-references in contracts that cannot all fit in the context window. Which strategy best preserves relevant detail while controlling prompt size?

stem: An assistant becomes less accurate during long conversations even though its prompt remains slightly below the advertised context limit. Logs show duplicated retrieval results, obsolete chat turns, and key instructions buried in the middle. What is the most likely explanation?

stem: A legal tool must answer questions about a 2,000-page set of contracts, which is far larger than the model's context window. Answers must quote exact clauses, and many clauses refer to other numbered sections. Which strategy fits best?
options: {'A': 'Split the contracts at section boundaries, retrieve the sections relevant to each question plus any sections they cite, and quote from those.', 'B': 'Split the contracts into fixed 500-token chunks, retrieve the five chunks most similar to each question, and quote from those.', 'C': 'Summarize each section in repeated rounds until all summaries fit, then answer each question and quote from the summaries.', 'D': 'Use the model with the largest context window, pass in as many pages as fit, and quote from whatever text is included.'}
rationale: Section-aware retrieval that follows cross-references keeps complete clauses verbatim within the window, while fixed chunks can split clauses and miss cited sections, summaries lose exact wording, and partial loading drops content.

rationale: The input fits within the window, and the position-dependent failure pattern matches weaker attention to the middle of long contexts, which is made worse when the question comes before the documents rather than after them.
